G1.brief: Write an approximately 800-word how-to guide for new craft cooperative operators completing one batch sort with the fictional Tavrel bead sorter.

facts.1: A baseline card supplies a known width reference.
facts.2: A route map assigns every width to exactly one outlet range.
facts.4: The baseline prevents reference drift from changing measurements.
facts.5: The route map prevents incorrect outlet delivery.
facts.6: Start with Ready status, clean dry beads, an empty tray, and the specified card.
facts.7: Step 4 loads only the intended batch.
facts.8: Step 1 seats and latches the empty tray.
facts.10: Step 3 selects and previews the route map.
facts.11: Clear Reference obscured by wiping the window and repeating calibration.
facts.12: Step 6 checks counts and saves a matching completion record.
facts.13: Step 2 reads the baseline card and checks Baseline ready.
facts.15: Step 5 starts sorting and waits for Batch complete.
facts.16: Kestrel contains 28 five-millimeter beads and 12 eight-millimeter beads.
facts.17: Kestrel uses Luma-6 and Loom Split with a six-millimeter boundary.
facts.18: Kestrel-04 must record 40 total, 28 at A, and 12 at B.

agentOnly.9: The scanner lamp has a 4,000-hour replacement interval.
agentOnly.14: Maintenance assigns route map revision checksums.

questions.a: Which action comes immediately after Step 4, loading the batch into the hopper?
questions.b: What should the operator do when Read reference reports Reference obscured?
questions.c: Does the baseline card determine which outlet receives each bead?
questions.d: Should a successful Kestrel-04 record show 40 beads overall, 28 at outlet A, and 12 at outlet B?

a.pass: Press Sort and wait for Batch complete, which is Step 5.

b.pass: Remove the card, wipe the scanner window with the supplied dry cloth, reinsert the card, and repeat Step 2 before loading beads.

c.pass: No; the route map determines outlet assignments.

d.pass: Yes; those are the required total and outlet counts.

checklist: Presents one complete batch sort in the six correct steps.
States the prerequisites and checks Baseline ready immediately after calibration.
Explains the separate purposes of the baseline card and route map.
Carries Kestrel through calibration, outlet setup, and completion verification using the exact settings and counts.
Includes the Reference obscured fix and omits maintainer details and unsupported claims.

G2.brief: Write an approximately 900-word conceptual lesson for trainee dispatchers learning usable capacity, queue ratio, and balanced transfer in the fictional Orvane parcel tram service.

facts.1: Usable capacity excludes reserved parcel spaces.
facts.2: Queue ratio divides waiting parcels by usable capacity.
facts.3: Balanced transfer reduces the larger ratio through permitted whole-parcel moves.
facts.5: A ratio above one means the current queue exceeds available spaces.
facts.6: Usable capacity prevents reserved spaces being counted as available.
facts.7: Queue ratio permits comparison across different tram sizes.
facts.8: Balanced transfer redistributes demand toward available room.
facts.9: The ratio denominator must exclude reserved spaces.
facts.10: Raw queue size alone does not establish relative demand.
facts.11: Transfers require matching destination and deadline before departure.
facts.12: Transfers preserve total parcels and both usable capacities.
facts.13: Recalculate both ratios after every parcel transfer.
facts.16: Nemi has six usable spaces and Pavo has twelve.
facts.17: Copper Loop starts with queues of twelve and six eligible parcels.
facts.18: Moving six parcels produces queues of six and twelve and equal ratios.

agentOnly.4: The simulator stores ratios to six decimal places.
agentOnly.15: Vesk Operations publishes quarterly reference tables.

questions.a: How is a tram's usable capacity calculated?
questions.b: Does the tram with the larger raw queue always have the larger queue ratio?
questions.c: Why does balanced transfer need queue ratio when comparing trams with different usable capacities?
questions.d: Would transferring only three parcels from Nemi to Pavo make their queue ratios equal in Copper Loop?

a.pass: Subtract reserved spaces from total parcel spaces.

b.pass: No; queue ratio also depends on usable capacity.

c.pass: Queue ratio expresses demand relative to usable capacity, so balanced transfer can compare differently sized trams and identify moves that reduce the larger relative load.
c.amended: Brief writer's key used any of ratio/relativ/proportion/normaliz/normalis; 'ratio' appears in the question, so any echo passed. Replaced before any build.

d.pass: No; three transfers leave ratios of 1.5 and 0.75, while six transfers produce equal ratios of one.

checklist: Explains the three concepts and the specific problem each solves.
Makes the dependency from usable capacity to queue ratio to balanced transfer explicit.
Uses Copper Loop to calculate capacities, compare initial ratios, and explain the six-parcel transfer.
Preserves transfer eligibility, whole-parcel moves, recalculation, and the stopping rule.
Omits maintainer details and introduces no unsupported operating rules.

G3.brief: Write an approximately 900-word tutorial for volunteer equipment librarians building and testing a small physical Dovren return board for three borrowed items.

facts.1: One identity token records one active loan's identifier, due day, and return mark.
facts.2: Due and Later depend on the current day, with Returned overriding dates.
facts.4: Identity tokens distinguish similar items and their loans.
facts.5: Date bands make loans needing attention visible without rereading dates.
facts.6: Building requires backing, pockets, cards, tape, a pen, and a current-day display.
facts.7: Step 3 attaches visible pockets beneath the headings.
facts.8: Step 1 labels the board and displays the starting day.
facts.10: Step 4 sorts sample tokens into their initial pockets.
facts.11: Day changes affect placement rather than recorded due dates.
facts.12: Step 2 creates the three unreturned identity tokens.
facts.13: Every token occupies one pocket and the visible count remains three.
facts.15: Step 5 advances the day, records a return, and checks the result.
facts.16: Temba starts on Day 12 with three specified item identifiers and due days.
facts.17: Initially Reel-3 is Due and the other two items are Later.
facts.18: After the test Reel-3 is Returned, Reel-8 is Due, and Reel-11 is Later.

agentOnly.3: Archived pocket outlines use a two-millimeter grid.
agentOnly.9: Pocket master width tolerance is one millimeter.
agentOnly.14: Pellis Pattern uses year and issue numbers for archive releases.

questions.a: Which action comes immediately after Step 2, making the identity tokens?
questions.b: Where does the finished board place each Temba item after the Day 13 test?
questions.c: Can two similar-looking items share one identity token while both loans are active?
questions.d: Should advancing the current-day card change the due dates written on the tokens?

a.pass: Attach one clear pocket beneath each column heading, which is Step 3.

b.pass: Reel-3 is in Returned, Reel-8 is in Due, and Reel-11 is in Later.
b.amended: Brief writer's key required only the words return, due, and later, which a mismatched answer also contains. Replaced before any build with one pattern per item.

c.pass: No; each active loan requires its own identity token.

d.pass: No; advancing the day can change placement but preserves the written due dates.

checklist: Builds and tests one complete physical board in the five correct steps.
Includes the materials and explains why identity tokens and date bands are needed.
Uses Temba identifiers and dates when making tokens, loading pockets, and testing the finished board.
Checks the exact final positions and three-token count while preserving the written due dates.
Explains the Returned override and omits maintainer details and unsupported features.
